title: Trigonometry
summary: Ratios, the standard-value table, the three identities, complementary angles, value-putting and max-min values. Tier 1 reliably holds 2-4 trig questions and they fall almost mechanically to the value table, one identity, or a 3-4-5 style triangle — among the cheapest marks in the paper.

subtopics.title: Ratios and standard values
subtopics.concept: In a right triangle, each acute angle has six ratios built from the three sides. Three are primary: sine, cosine, tangent; three are their reciprocals. Five standard angles cover almost every exam question, and one known ratio produces all six.

Cosine reverses the row: $\cos60^\circ=\dfrac12$; $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ is $\cos30^\circ$.
$\sec$ pairs with $\cos$; $\text{cosec}$ pairs with $\sin$. Both flip, nothing more.
Exact fractions keep the triplet visible and the arithmetic short.

subtopics.notes:
### The six ratios
For an acute angle $\theta$ in a right triangle:
- $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$
- $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}$
- $\tan\theta=\dfrac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}$

The other three flip these: $\text{cosec}=\dfrac{1}{\sin}$, $\sec=\dfrac{1}{\cos}$, $\cot=\dfrac{1}{\tan}$.

> **Rule:** Name the sides from the angle you are using. The opposite side changes when the angle changes.

### The standard table, built not memorised
Write $\sin$ as $\dfrac{\sqrt{k}}{2}$ for $k=0,1,2,3,4$:
| $\theta$ | $0^\circ$ | $30^\circ$ | $45^\circ$ | $60^\circ$ | $90^\circ$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $\sin$ | $0$ | $\dfrac12$ | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $1$ |
| $\cos$ | $1$ | $\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$ | $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ | $\dfrac12$ | $0$ |

$\cos$ is $\sin$ read backwards. Then $\tan=\dfrac{\sin}{\cos}$ gives $0,\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3},1,\sqrt3$ and undefined at $90^\circ$.

Read $\tan$ straight off that division: it starts at $0$, passes $1$ exactly at $45^\circ$, and blows up where cosine hits zero. A one-line check: $\tan30^\circ\tan60^\circ=1$, which the table confirms because the angles are complementary.

> **Tip:** Recompute the row from $\sqrt{k}/2$ instead of memorising. It cannot be forgotten in the hall.

### One ratio makes all six
Given $\sin\theta=\dfrac35$: opposite $3$, hypotenuse $5$, so adjacent $4$ (the $3$-$4$-$5$ triangle). Then $\cos=\dfrac45$, $\tan=\dfrac34$, $\text{cosec}=\dfrac53$, $\sec=\dfrac54$, $\cot=\dfrac43$.

The Pythagoras step is the whole work: two sides known means the third follows.

Try the same move with $\cos\theta=\dfrac{5}{13}$: adjacent $5$, hypotenuse $13$, so the opposite side is $12$ from the $5$-$12$-$13$ triplet. Then $\tan\theta=\dfrac{12}{5}$, $\sec\theta=\dfrac{13}{5}$, $\cot\theta=\dfrac{5}{12}$ and $\cosec\theta=\dfrac{13}{12}$. Six answers come from one fact.

> **Watch:** Keep the given ratio's fraction exact. Decimal sides break the triplets ($3$-$4$-$5$, $5$-$12$-$13$, $20$-$21$-$29$).

### Labelling a given triangle
Triangle right-angled at $B$ with $AB=5$, $BC=12$: hypotenuse $AC=13$. For angle $A$, the opposite side is $BC=12$, so $\sin A=\dfrac{12}{13}$.

Switch to angle $C$ and the roles swap: $\sin C=\dfrac{5}{13}$. One drawing, two readings.

### Reading an angle off a value
$2\sin\theta=\sqrt3$ means $\sin\theta=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{2}$, which is the $60^\circ$ entry. Equations of this shape just run the table backwards.

The reverse lookup needs the function named first: the value $\dfrac12$ means $30^\circ$ for sine but $60^\circ$ for cosine, while $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}$ means $45^\circ$ for both. Options are often rationalised, so know $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}=\dfrac{\sqrt3}{3}$ too.

> **Remember:** Every ratio value in this range belongs to exactly one standard angle, so match it and stop.

subtopics.title: Fundamental identities
subtopics.concept: Three identities drive nearly every simplification: sine squared plus cosine squared equals one, and its tan-sec and cot-cosec cousins. Conjugate pairs turn sums into reciprocals, and squaring a sum removes the cross terms.

formulas.name: Reciprocal products
formulas.note: The constant that kills cross terms.

tricks.title: Sum given, difference taken
tricks.body: sec + tan = 5 means sec - tan = 1/5, because their product is 1. Then add or subtract the pair.

tricks.title: Divide through by cosine
tricks.body: A sin-cos fraction becomes a tan fraction when every term is divided by cosine. Substitute tan and finish.

tricks.title: Square and subtract two
tricks.body: tan + cot = 5: square it, use tan times cot = 1, and the squared sum is 25 - 2.

Divide every term of numerator and denominator, then substitute $\tan$.
The sum is $1$; the $2$ appears only after adding both squared sums.
Reciprocal pairs multiply to $1$, never anything else.

subtopics.notes:
### The three engines
$$\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta=1,\qquad 1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta,\qquad 1+\cot^2\theta=\cosec^2\theta$$
Divide the first by $\cos^2\theta$ and the second appears; divide by $\sin^2\theta$ for the third. One identity, three costumes.

Verify with $\theta=30^\circ$: $\sin^2+\cos^2=\dfrac14+\dfrac34=1$ holds, and $1+\tan^230^\circ=1+\dfrac13=\dfrac43=\sec^230^\circ$. Checks like this catch a misremembered formula instantly.

> **Rule:** Spot which squared pair the question shows, then apply the matching engine and cancel.

### Conjugate pairs
$$(\sec\theta+\tan\theta)(\sec\theta-\tan\theta)=\sec^2\theta-\tan^2\theta=1$$
So the two factors are reciprocals. Given $\sec+\tan=5$, the partner is $\dfrac15$. Adding the two: $2\sec=5+\dfrac15=\dfrac{26}{5}$, so $\sec=\dfrac{13}{5}$ and $\tan=\dfrac{12}{5}$.

The same trick works for $\cosec+\cot$: the conjugate product is also $1$.

Numbers stay friendly here. $\cosec\theta+\cot\theta=\dfrac52$ forces $\cosec\theta-\cot\theta=\dfrac25$; adding, $2\cosec\theta=\dfrac{29}{10}$, so $\cosec\theta=\dfrac{29}{20}$ and $\sin\theta=\dfrac{20}{29}$. The $20$-$21$-$29$ triplet was hiding inside the fractions.

> **Tip:** A 'sum given, difference asked' question is this pair in disguise. Write the product-of-difference identity before anything else.

### Squares of sums
$(a+b)^2+(a-b)^2=2(a^2+b^2)$, so
$$(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2+(\sin\theta-\cos\theta)^2=2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)=2$$
Check: each square expands to $1\pm2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, and the cross terms cancel.

The same square bridges a given sum to a product: $\sin\theta+\cos\theta=\dfrac75$ squares to $1+2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\dfrac{49}{25}$, so $\sin\theta\cos\theta=\dfrac{12}{25}$. The product falls out of the square every time.

### Build tan by dividing by cos
Any fraction of sines and cosines becomes a fraction of tangents after dividing top and bottom by $\cos\theta$:
$$\frac{4\sin\theta-\cos\theta}{4\cos\theta+\sin\theta}=\frac{4\tan\theta-1}{4+\tan\theta}$$
With $\tan\theta=\dfrac34$: numerator $3-1=2$, denominator $4+\dfrac34=\dfrac{19}{4}$, so the value is $\dfrac{8}{19}$.

> **Watch:** Divide every term, top and bottom. A missed term breaks the whole fraction.

### Squared sums from a given sum
$\tan\theta+\cot\theta=5$. Square: $\tan^2+\cot^2+2\tan\cot=25$, and $\tan\cot=1$, so $\tan^2+\cot^2=23$.

The same layout gives $\sin+\cosec$ questions: square, use the product $1$, subtract $2$. For instance $\sin\theta+\cosec\theta=3$ squares to $\sin^2+\cosec^2+2=9$, so $\sin^2+\cosec^2=7$.

> **Remember:** Products of reciprocal pairs are always $1$: $\sin\cdot\cosec$, $\cos\cdot\sec$, $\tan\cdot\cot$. That is where terms vanish.

subtopics.title: Complementary angles
subtopics.concept: Angles adding to 90 degrees swap each ratio with its co-partner: sine becomes cosine, tangent becomes cotangent, secant becomes cosecant. This single swap collapses long sums, product chains and paired differences, and it solves for unknown angles by matching partners.

formulas.name: Complementary swaps
formulas.note: Drop the co- or add it.

formulas.name: Right triangle angles
formulas.note: The two acute angles are partners.

tricks.title: Sum the angles first
tricks.body: Before computing anything, add the two angles. Ninety degrees means the terms are twins.

tricks.title: Chains pair from the ends
tricks.body: tan 5 with tan 85, tan 25 with tan 65: each pair multiplies to 1, and the lone tan 45 is 1.

tricks.title: Match partners to find the angle
tricks.body: sin of something = cos of something: the two somethings must add to 90. That gives a linear equation.

mistakes.right: The complement swaps to cosine: $\cos\theta$. No swap, no collapse.
Partners are $\sin\leftrightarrow\cos$, $\tan\leftrightarrow\cot$, $\sec\leftrightarrow\cosec$.

mistakes.right: Unpaired middle terms still contribute their value; $45^\circ$ contributes $1$.

mistakes.wrong: Leaving answers in degrees and radians mixed.
mistakes.right: Exam angles are degrees; keep the symbol consistent throughout.

subtopics.notes:
### The swap rules
For complementary angles, $\theta$ and $90^\circ-\theta$:
$$\sin(90^\circ-\theta)=\cos\theta,\quad \tan(90^\circ-\theta)=\cot\theta,\quad \sec(90^\circ-\theta)=\cosec\theta$$
The 'co-' in cosine literally means 'complement's sine'. Any ratio of one angle equals the co-ratio of its partner.

Check at $\theta=35^\circ$: $\sin35^\circ=\cos55^\circ$, and $\tan35^\circ\tan55^\circ=1$ because the tangents are reciprocal partners. One complement, three identities confirmed on the spot.

> **Rule:** In a right triangle the two acute angles are complementary, so each angle's sine is the other's cosine.

### Collapsing sums
$$\sin35^\circ\sec55^\circ+\cos35^\circ\cosec55^\circ$$
$\sec55^\circ=\dfrac{1}{\cos55^\circ}=\dfrac{1}{\sin35^\circ}$, so the first term is $1$. The second term is $1$ the same way. Total: $2$.

Convert everything to one angle, then watch the expression fold.

Another shape: $\dfrac{\cos25^\circ}{\sec65^\circ}+\dfrac{\sin25^\circ}{\cosec65^\circ}$. Since $\cos65^\circ=\sin25^\circ$, the first fraction is $\cos25^\circ\sin25^\circ$; the second equals the same product. The sum is $2\sin25^\circ\cos25^\circ=\sin50^\circ$.

> **Tip:** Choose one target angle (say $35^\circ$) and rewrite every piece in it before simplifying.

### Product chains
$\tan5^\circ\tan85^\circ=1$ because the angles are complementary. So:
$$\tan5^\circ\tan25^\circ\tan45^\circ\tan65^\circ\tan85^\circ=1\times1\times1=1$$
Chains pair off from the ends; the middle $45^\circ$ term is $1$ on its own. Four-factor chains work identically: $\tan10^\circ\tan20^\circ\tan70^\circ\tan80^\circ=1$, since $10+80=90$ and $20+70=90$.

### Twin differences die
$\cosec68^\circ-\sec22^\circ$: since $68^\circ+22^\circ=90^\circ$, $\cosec68^\circ=\sec22^\circ$. The difference is exactly $0$.

Sums of twins double instead of vanishing: $\sec72^\circ+\cosec18^\circ=2\cosec18^\circ$. And a long chain like $\tan1^\circ\tan2^\circ\cdots\tan89^\circ$ pairs into $44$ ones around the middle $\tan45^\circ=1$, so the whole product is $1$.

> **Watch:** Check the angle sum first. If it is $90^\circ$, the answer may need no computation at all.

### Solving for the angle
$\sin3A=\cos(A-10^\circ)$: the partners rule needs $3A=90^\circ-(A-10^\circ)$, so $4A=100^\circ$ and $A=25^\circ$. Check: $\sin75^\circ=\cos15^\circ$.

Same layout with tangents: $\tan2A=\cot(3A-10^\circ)$ gives $2A+3A-10^\circ=90^\circ$, so $A=20^\circ$. A negative argument also resolves: $\sin(2A-10^\circ)=\cos(3A+20^\circ)$ gives $5A+10^\circ=90^\circ$, so $A=16^\circ$.

> **Remember:** Convert the cosine or cotangent to its partner first, then solve the plain linear equation in the angle.

subtopics.title: Value-putting and given-ratio questions
subtopics.concept: Value-putting questions hand you a ratio or a condition and ask for an expression. Two moves cover them: substitute standard angle values directly, or draw the triangle the condition describes and read the expression off it.

tricks.body: cos squared 30 and sin squared 60 are the same number; scan for such twins before computing.

subtopics.notes:
### Put the standard values in
$2\tan^2 45^\circ+\cos^2 30^\circ-\sin^2 60^\circ$: with $\tan45^\circ=1$ and both $30^\circ$/$60^\circ$ squared terms equal to $\dfrac34$:
$$2+\frac34-\frac34=2$$
Notice how $\cos^2 30^\circ$ and $\sin^2 60^\circ$ cancel by symmetry before any arithmetic.

One more: $\sin^230^\circ+\tan^245^\circ+\cos^260^\circ=\dfrac14+1+\dfrac14=\dfrac32$. Substitute first, add the fractions second, and the answer arrives without any identity at all.

> **Rule:** Replace every ratio first, simplify second. Half of these questions cancel themselves.

### sin + cos given
Square the given sum: $(\sin\theta+\cos\theta)^2=1+2\sin\theta\cos\theta$. So with the sum $=\sqrt2$:
$$2\sin\theta\cos\theta=2-1=1\Rightarrow\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac12$$
The same square gives $\sin\theta-\cos\theta$ when the sum is known (watch the sign). With $\sin+\cos=\dfrac75$ the difference squares to $1-2\sin\cos=1-\dfrac{24}{25}=\dfrac{1}{25}$, so $|\sin-\cos|=\dfrac15$.

> **Tip:** $\sin+\cos=\sqrt2$ happens only at $45^\circ$; the product $\dfrac12$ confirms it.

### tan condition into a fraction
$5\tan\theta=4$ and the fraction $\dfrac{5\sin\theta-3\cos\theta}{5\sin\theta+3\cos\theta}$. Divide top and bottom by $\cos\theta$:
$$\frac{5\tan\theta-3}{5\tan\theta+3}=\frac{4-3}{4+3}=\frac17$$
The condition turns the whole expression into one number.

### cot or tan fraction: draw the triangle
$\cot\theta=\dfrac{21}{20}$: adjacent $21$, opposite $20$, hypotenuse $\sqrt{441+400}=29$. Then $\cos\theta=\dfrac{21}{29}$ directly.

The triplet $20$-$21$-$29$ was hiding inside the fraction. Drawing beats manipulating.

With $\tan\theta=\dfrac{4}{3}$ instead, the same $3$-$4$-$5$ drawing hands over $\sec\theta=\dfrac{5}{4}$ and $\cosec\theta=\dfrac{5}{3}$ at a glance. The triangle keeps paying rent.

> **Watch:** For $\cot$ the first number is the adjacent side, not the opposite. That single slip flips every answer.

### Sum of reciprocal partners
$\cosec\theta+\cot\theta=3$. The conjugate is $\dfrac13$, so $2\cosec\theta=3+\dfrac13=\dfrac{10}{3}$, giving $\cosec\theta=\dfrac53$ and $\sin\theta=\dfrac35$.

One reciprocal move, no quadratic.

The pair also splits a value the other way: $\sec\theta+\tan\theta=3$ gives $\sec\theta-\tan\theta=\dfrac13$, hence $\sec\theta=\dfrac{5}{3}$ and $\tan\theta=\dfrac{4}{3}$. Add or subtract the pair, and the individuals appear.

> **Remember:** Value-putting never needs to solve for $\theta$ itself. The ratio travels, the angle never appears.

subtopics.title: Maximum and minimum values
subtopics.concept: On zero to ninety degrees, sine and cosine stay between zero and one, while secant and cosecant stay at one or above. A sine-cosine combination peaks at the square root of a squared plus b squared, and reciprocal pairs bottom out at two by AM-GM.

formulas.name: Amplitude of a sin + b cos
formulas.note: General angles; on 0 to 90 check the endpoints too.

formulas.name: AM-GM floor
formulas.note: For positive x; equality when x = 1.

formulas.name: Weighted squares
formulas.note: Rewrite as one constant plus one square.

tricks.title: Square, add, root
tricks.body: The maximum of a sin + b cos is the hypotenuse of the a-b right triangle. 4 and 3 give 5.

tricks.title: AM-GM floor of two
tricks.body: Anything plus its own reciprocal bottoms at 2: tan + cot, sec + cosec, all the same.

tricks.title: Weighted squares: constant plus square
tricks.body: Rewrite 5 sin squared + 12 cos squared as 5 + 7 cos squared. The range is then obvious.

mistakes.right: The peak is $\sqrt{16+9}=5$; the functions never peak together.
The product tops at $\dfrac12$ at $45^\circ$, since it equals $\dfrac{\sin2\theta}{2}$.
The floor is $4$: the squares push it above the plain AM-GM pair.
Only beyond $45^\circ$; below it cosine is larger.
$5\sin^2+12\cos^2$ is smallest when the weight sits on the smaller value: $5$ at $90^\circ$.

subtopics.notes:
### The ranges
| Function | Range on $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ |
|---|---|
| $\sin\theta,\ \cos\theta$ | $0$ to $1$ |
| $\sec\theta,\ \cosec\theta$ | $1$ or more |
| $\tan\theta,\ \cot\theta$ | $0$ onwards, unbounded |

$\sin0^\circ=0$ rises to $\sin90^\circ=1$; cosine runs the other way. They cross exactly once, at $45^\circ$.

The table also explains why $\cosec\theta$ never lands between $0$ and $1$: it is $\dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}$ and $\sin\theta\le1$. The same logic lifts $\sec\theta$ to $1$ or above.

> **Rule:** $\sin\theta>\cos\theta$ holds precisely when $\theta>45^\circ$; below it, cosine leads.

### The amplitude rule
$$-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}\le a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta\le\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$$
$4\sin\theta+3\cos\theta$ peaks at $\sqrt{16+9}=5$. The maximum of $a\sin+b\cos$ never needs calculus: square, add, root.

On the full circle the minimum is $-\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$; restricted to acute angles the low end is the smaller of $a$ and $b$, hit at an endpoint. For $4\sin+3\cos$ on $0^\circ$ to $90^\circ$ the range is $[3,5]$. Read the domain before answering.

> **Tip:** The peak of $a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta$ answers half this subtopic. Compute $a^2+b^2$ first.

### Products of sin and cos
$$\sin\theta\cos\theta=\frac{\sin2\theta}{2}\le\frac12$$
$2\sin\theta\cos\theta=\sin2\theta$ tops at $1$, so $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ tops at $\dfrac12$, both at $45^\circ$.

Any question about 'maximum of sin times cos' is this line in disguise.

### AM-GM floors
For positive $x$: $x+\dfrac1x\ge2$. So:
- $\tan\theta+\cot\theta\ge2$ (product $1$)
- $\sec\theta+\cosec\theta\ge2$
- $\sec^2\theta+\cosec^2\theta\ge4$, since it equals $\dfrac{1}{\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta}$ and $\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta\le\dfrac14$

Each floor is attained where the two terms balance, at $45^\circ$. Equality pins the angle exactly: $\tan\theta+\cot\theta=2$ forces $\tan\theta=1$, hence $\theta=45^\circ$. The floor and the balance point arrive together.

> **Watch:** Secant and cosecant never fall below $1$, so their sums have higher floors. Squares shift the floor again.

### Weighted sin-squared and cos-squared
$5\sin^2\theta+12\cos^2\theta=5+7\cos^2\theta$. Since $0\le\cos^2\theta\le1$, the expression lives in $[5,12]$: minimum $5$, maximum $12$.

The endpoints occur at $90^\circ$ (all sine) and $0^\circ$ (all cosine). Try $7\sin^2\theta+2\cos^2\theta=2+5\sin^2\theta$, which lives in $[2,7]$: the rewrite is mechanical whichever way the weights lean.

> **Remember:** Rewrite the mix as one constant plus one squared term. The range reads off in one line, no differentiation.

patterns.name: Max and min of a sin plus b cos
patterns.howToSpot: A linear mix of sine and cosine; an extreme asked.
steps: Take the square root for the amplitude.
patterns.why: The amplitude formula replaces all calculus for this expression family.

patterns.name: Bounds of sin times cos
patterns.howToSpot: A product or double of sin and cos; its maximum asked.
patterns.why: The double-angle rewrite turns the product into a single bounded function.

example.q: The maximum value of $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:

patterns.name: AM-GM self-reciprocal sums
patterns.howToSpot: A sum of a function and its reciprocal; a minimum asked.
steps: Confirm the product of the terms is $1$.
patterns.why: Reciprocal pairs always balance at their floor, which AM-GM locates instantly.

patterns.name: Ordering and crossover comparisons
patterns.howToSpot: When is sin greater than cos, or tan greater than one.
steps: Below it cosine leads; above it sine leads.
patterns.why: All such comparisons pivot on the single $45^\circ$ crossing, so one fact answers many questions.

patterns.name: Weighted sin-squared plus cos-squared range
patterns.howToSpot: A weighted mix of squared sine and cosine; min and max asked.
steps: Rewrite as constant plus weight times one square.
patterns.why: The rewrite makes the range a one-step reading exercise with no calculus.

example.q: The minimum and maximum of $5\sin^2\theta + 12\cos^2\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) are:

revision: Ranges: $\sin,\cos\in[0,1]$; $\sec,\cosec\ge1$; $\tan,\cot$ unbounded.
$\max(a\sin+b\cos)=\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$; square, add, root.
$\sin\theta\cos\theta\le\dfrac12$; $\sin2\theta\le1$.
$x+\dfrac1x\ge2$ floors: $\tan+\cot\ge2$, $\sec^2+\cosec^2\ge4$.
Weighted squares: rewrite as constant plus square, read the range.
$\sin=\cos$ only at $45^\circ$; that is the ordering crossover.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A sum/difference/product of sin/cos/tan (often sec/cosec/cot too) at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, 90° asked as one value.
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert every function to its table value via the $\frac{\sqrt{k}}{2}$ construction (reciprocals for sec/cosec/cot), then compute with exact fractions. Keep surds as surds; rationalise only the final answer.

pyqPatterns.pattern: One ratio given → the rest of the triangle
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'If sinθ = 3/5 find tanθ' style — one ratio (sometimes surd form), other ratios asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Draw the right triangle from the given ratio, complete the third side by Pythagoras (expect a triplet), and read the asked ratio off the same triangle w.r.t. the named angle.

example.q: If $\cosec\theta = \frac{13}{5}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan\theta$ is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'If secθ + tanθ = m, find secθ − tanθ' — or the pair subtracted/added to extract an individual ratio.
pyqPatterns.approach: $(\sec\theta + \tan\theta)(\sec\theta - \tan\theta) = 1$, so the conjugate is its reciprocal $\frac{1}{m}$. Adding/subtracting the pair gives $2\sec\theta$ and $2\tan\theta$ individually; a triangle then returns sin/cos.

example.q: If $\cosec\theta + \cot\theta = 3$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\cosec\theta - \cot\theta$ is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A sum (or difference) of sin and cos given as m; the product sinθcosθ, the opposite difference, or a cubic combination asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Square the given: $\sin\theta\cos\theta = \frac{m^2-1}{2}$; $(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 = 2 - m^2$; cubes via $x^3+y^3=(x+y)(x^2-xy+y^2)$. Sub-specials: $m = \sqrt2$ → product $\frac12$; $m = 1$ → product $0$.

pyqPatterns.pattern: tanθ given → linear fraction in sin and cos
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: tanθ = p/q (or 5tanθ = 4 style); a fraction like (a·sinθ + b·cosθ)/(c·cosθ + d·sinθ) asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Divide numerator and denominator by $\cos\theta$: the fraction becomes $\frac{a\tan\theta + b}{c + d\tan\theta}$. Substitute $t = \frac{p}{q}$ exactly (fractions, not decimals) and simplify once.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Angles pair to 90° (35 & 55, 20 & 70...) across different functions — or a long tangent chain with 45° in the middle.
pyqPatterns.approach: Flip one function of each pair: $\sec 55^\circ = \frac{1}{\sin 35^\circ}$ etc.; products like $\tan\theta\tan(90^\circ-\theta) = 1$. Chains $\tan 1^\circ \cdots \tan 89^\circ$ collapse to 1. Difference-of-twins questions ($\cos 50^\circ - \sin 40^\circ$) are instantly 0.

example.solution: Pairs: $10+80 = 90$ and $20+70 = 90$; each pair multiplies to 1, so the product is 1.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'If sin 3A = cos(A − 10°), find A' — different functions at related angles, one unknown.
pyqPatterns.approach: Force the same function ($\cos x = \sin(90^\circ - x)$) or use the shortcut: complementary-function arguments sum to $90^\circ$. Solve the resulting linear equation; sanity-check the angle keeps all arguments in range.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the maximum of 4sinθ + 3cosθ' — Pythagorean coefficients; minimum may be asked instead.
pyqPatterns.approach: Max $= +\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$, min $= -\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$ (unrestricted θ); with $0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ$ check endpoints too. Expect triplets: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Minimum of tan²+cot², sec²+cosec², tan+cot — or the max of sinθcosθ / 2sinθcosθ.

example.q: The minimum value of $\tan\theta + \cot\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:

pyqPatterns.pattern: Two sides of the right triangle → a named ratio
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two sides given (or hyp + one leg); sin/cos/tan of one acute angle asked — the angle described in words ('opposite the longer leg').
pyqPatterns.approach: Third side by Pythagoras, then attach opposite/adjacent to the NAMED angle — 'opposite the shorter leg' is the smaller angle. Triplet multiples supply the exam numbers.

example.q: In a right triangle, the legs adjacent to and opposite an acute angle are $15$ cm and $8$ cm. The hypotenuse is:

solvedExamples.shortcut: Recognise the form: $\frac{2t}{1-t^2}=\tan2\theta$ with $\theta=30^\circ$ → $\tan60^\circ=\sqrt3$, no fractions at all.

solvedExamples.q: If $\cos\theta=\dfrac{7}{25}$, then the value of $\tan\theta$ is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet: see 7 and 25, write 24 instantly. Trap: $\frac{7}{24}$ is $\cot\theta$.

solvedExamples.solution:
Pair $\tan\theta$ with $\tan(90^\circ-\theta)=\cot\theta$: each pair multiplies to 1.

44 such pairs plus $\tan45^\circ=1$ give the product 1.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Every angle pairs with its complement; middle term is $\tan45^\circ=1$. Product $=1$.
Reduce each bracket to a single fraction; the $\sin^2\cos^2$ cancels completely → 1. (Check at $45^\circ$: $(\frac{1}{\sqrt2})^2\times2=1$.)

solvedExamples.solution:
$a\sin\theta+b\cos\theta$ peaks at $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}$: here $\sqrt{3^2+4^2}=5$ (at $\tan\theta=\frac34$).

So the greatest value of the expression is $5+5=10$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: $\sqrt{a^2+b^2}=5$ for the trig part, then add the constant: $5+5=10$. Trap: 12 (added $3+4+5$ directly).
solvedExamples.pattern: max of a sin + b cos + c

practice.shortcut: Read the table: $\frac12+\frac12+1=2$. $\cot45^\circ=1$, not 0.
$\sec^2-\tan^2=1$ (identity pair), then $1-\sin^2=\cos^2$.
This is $\sin(60+30)=\sin90^\circ=1$ — recognise the sine-addition shape instead of multiplying.
5-12-13 triplet → $\frac{5}{12}$. Trap: $\frac{12}{5}$ is $\cot\theta$.
Divide through by $\cos\theta$: $(t+1)/(t-1)$ with $t=\frac34$ → $-7$. (Same trick works for any sin/cos ratio expression.)
practice.pattern: divide by cos to use tan

practice.q: If $\sin(40^\circ+\theta)=\cos(30^\circ+\theta)$, where both angles are acute, then $\theta$ equals:
practice.shortcut: Sum to 90: $70+2\theta=90$ → $\theta=10^\circ$. Trap: 20 (forgot to halve).
practice.pattern: sin A = cos B angle equation

practice.q: If $\sin\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$, then the value of $\cos^2\theta+\cos^4\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
From the condition, $\sin^2\theta=1-\sin\theta$, so $\cos^2\theta=1-\sin^2\theta=\sin\theta$.

Then $\cos^4\theta=\sin^2\theta=1-\sin\theta$.

Sum $=\sin\theta+1-\sin\theta=1$.
practice.shortcut: $\cos^2=\sin$ and $\cos^4=\sin^2=1-\sin$ → total 1, without ever finding $\theta$.

practice.q: The minimum value of $\sin\theta+\cos\theta$ for $0^\circ\le\theta\le90^\circ$ is:
practice.solution: $\sin\theta+\cos\theta$ ranges from 1 (at $\theta=0^\circ$ or $90^\circ$) to $\sqrt2$ (at $45^\circ$). The minimum is 1.
practice.shortcut: Range $[1,\sqrt2]$: min 1, max $\sqrt2$. Trap: $\sqrt2$ is the **maximum**.
Complementary pairs collapse; $\tan45^\circ=1$ stands alone.
The $s^2c^2$ terms cancel exactly: $-6+6=0$ → answer 0 for every $\theta$. (Try $\theta=45^\circ$ to confirm.)
5-12-13: $\sin=\frac5{13}$ → cosec $=\frac{13}{5}$ (flip). Trap: $\frac{13}{12}$ is $\sec\theta$.

practice.q: The minimum value of $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta$ (for acute $\theta$) is:
practice.solution:
By AM–GM, $4\tan^2\theta+9\cot^2\theta\ge2\sqrt{4\times9}=12$,

with equality when $2\tan\theta=3\cot\theta$, i.e. $\tan^2\theta=\frac32$ (reachable since tan is unbounded).
practice.shortcut: $2\sqrt{ab}=2\sqrt{36}=12$. Trap: 6 is $\sqrt{ab}$ (forgot to double), 13 is $a+b$.
Companion is $\frac1k=\frac13$; average the pair: cosec $=\frac{3+\frac13}{2}=\frac53$ → $\sin=\frac35$.

practice.solution:
Write the brackets as $[t+(s-1)][t-(s-1)]=t^2-(s-1)^2$ where $t=\tan\theta$, $s=\sec\theta$.

$=t^2-s^2+2s-1=-1+2s-1=2(\sec\theta-1)$, using $s^2-t^2=1$.
practice.shortcut: Difference of squares, then $t^2-s^2=-1$: answer $2(\sec\theta-1)$. Quick check at $30^\circ$: LHS $\approx0.309$ = RHS.

practice.solution:
Write the left side as $2(\sin^2\theta+\cos^2\theta)+5\cos^2\theta=2+5\cos^2\theta$.

So $2+5\cos^2\theta=6\Rightarrow\cos^2\theta=\frac45$, hence $\sin^2\theta=\frac15$.

$\tan^2\theta=\frac{\sin^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}=\frac{1/5}{4/5}=\frac14\Rightarrow\tan\theta=\frac12$ (acute).
practice.shortcut: Anchor to $a(\sin^2+\cos^2)+(b-a)\cos^2$: solve for $\cos^2$, then $\tan^2=\frac{1-\cos^2}{\cos^2}$. Traps: 2 (reciprocal), $\frac14$ ($\tan^2$, forgot the root).
Complementary twins: both read $\frac{\sqrt1}{2}$. Trap: $\frac12$ (evaluating only one term).
$1 + 1 - 1 = 1$. Trap: $2$ (forgetting the coefficient is already consumed).
Both terms are $\sqrt3$. Trap: $\sqrt3$ (assuming they cancel or one is $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}$).

practice.q: If $\sin\theta = \frac{3}{5}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\tan = \frac{3}{4}$. Trap: $\frac43$ (tan of the OTHER acute angle).

practice.q: If $\cos\theta = \frac{12}{13}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sec\theta - \tan\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{13}{12} - \frac{5}{12} = \frac23$. Trap: $\frac{5}{12}$ — that is $\tan\theta$ itself.

practice.q: If $\tan\theta = \frac{1}{\sqrt{7}}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\cosec^2\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\cosec^2 = 1 + \cot^2 = 1 + 7 = 8$ — the identity does it in one line. Trap: $\sqrt8$ (forgot to square).

practice.q: In $\triangle ABC$ right-angled at $B$, $AB = 5$ cm and $BC = 12$ cm. The value of $\sin A$ is:
practice.solution: AC $= \sqrt{25 + 144} = 13$. Side opposite to $A$ is $BC = 12$: $\sin A = \frac{12}{13}$.
practice.shortcut: Opposite to A is BC, not AB. Trap: $\frac{5}{13}$ (reading the wrong leg as opposite).

practice.q: In a right triangle the hypotenuse is $25$ cm and one leg is $7$ cm. The cosine of the angle opposite the $7$ cm leg is:
practice.solution:
Third leg $= \sqrt{625 - 49} = 24$ (7-24-25). The angle opposite $7$ has adjacent leg $24$:

$\cos = \frac{24}{25}$.
practice.shortcut: Opposite 7 → adjacent is 24 → $\cos = \frac{24}{25}$. Trap: $\frac{7}{25}$ (that is the SINE of the same angle).
$2 + 2 = 4$. Trap: $2$ (assuming the two terms cancel or equal 1).

practice.solution:
$\sec^2\theta - \tan^2\theta = 1$ for every $\theta$ where defined — the answer is $1$ without any table work.

(Indeed $\sec^2 30^\circ = \frac43$, $\tan^2 30^\circ = \frac13$.)
practice.shortcut: The identity $\sec^2 - \tan^2 = 1$ is angle-independent. Trap: $\frac13$ — computing entries and slipping.

practice.q: If $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 5$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sec\theta - \tan\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: Conjugate = reciprocal: $\frac15$. Trap: $4$ (subtracting instead of using the product).

practice.q: If $\sec\theta + \tan\theta = 5$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
Subtract the conjugate: $2\tan\theta = 5 - \frac15 = \frac{24}{5}$ → $\tan\theta = \frac{12}{5}$.

(5-12-13 triangle: $\sin\theta = \frac{5}{13}$ if ever asked.)
practice.shortcut: $\tan = \frac{m - 1/m}{2} = \frac{12}{5}$. Trap: $\frac{5}{12}$ — the inverse fraction.
Cross terms cancel: $2$. Trap: $1$ (using $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ and forgetting the second bracket).
Convert all three, cancel to $1$. Trap: $0$ (assuming one bracket vanishes — none does).
$\frac{4t - 1}{4 + t} = \frac{8}{19}$. Trap: $\frac{8}{13}$ (using $t = \frac34$ as $t = \frac43$).
$\frac{2t+1}{t-2} = 7$. Trap: $-7$ — a sign slip reading $t - 2$ as $2 - t$.
$\tan = 1$ at $45^\circ$ only. Trap: $90^\circ$ (where $\sin = 1$, $\cos = 0$ — not equal).

practice.q: If $\sin\theta + \cosec\theta = 2$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sin^2\theta + \cosec^2\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: The sum 2 forces $\sin\theta = 1$: both squares are 1. Trap: $4$ (squaring the given sum).
Squaring $s^2 + c^2 = 1$ is the whole proof. Trap: $1$ — true only when one function is zero.

practice.solution:
Cube the identity: $(\sin^2\theta + \cos^2\theta)^3 = 1$ expands to

$\sin^6\theta + \cos^6\theta + 3\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta = 1$, so the sum is $1 - 3\sin^2\theta\cos^2\theta$.
practice.shortcut: $x^3 + y^3 = (x+y)^3 - 3xy(x+y)$ with $x+y = 1$. Trap: $1 - 2s^2c^2$ — that is the FOURTH-power form.

practice.q: If $\tan\theta + \cot\theta = 2$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\tan\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
$x + \frac1x = 2$ forces $x = 1$ (a positive number and its reciprocal sum to 2 only at equality).

So $\tan\theta = 1$, i.e. $\theta = 45^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $x + \frac{1}{x} \ge 2$ with equality only at $x = 1$. Trap: $2$ (confusing the sum with the value).

practice.q: If $\sec\theta - \tan\theta = \frac{1}{3}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sec\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: Average the pair: $\frac{3 + \frac13}{2} = \frac53$. Trap: $\frac{10}{3}$ (forgot to halve).
Twins cancel. Trap: $1$ or $\frac12$ — treating them as unrelated values.
Both flip to reciprocals: $1 + 1 = 2$. Trap: $1$ (cancelling only one pair).
$22 + 68 = 90$: identical twins. Trap: $\sec 22^\circ$ (dropping the second term).
Pair the ends: $1$. Trap: $0$ — nothing here is zero; every factor is finite and positive.
Two pairs: $1 \times 1 = 1$. Trap: $\frac{1}{3}$ (squaring the 30-60 pair instead of multiplying).
$4A = 100$: $A = 25^\circ$. Trap: $20^\circ$ (dropping the $-10^\circ$).

practice.solution:
$\sec x = \cosec(90^\circ - x)$: the arguments must satisfy $2\theta + \theta + 30^\circ = 90^\circ$.

$3\theta = 60^\circ$ → $\theta = 20^\circ$.
practice.shortcut: $3\theta = 60$: $\theta = 20^\circ$. Trap: $30^\circ$ (setting $2\theta = \theta + 30$, the wrong pairing).
$2\theta = 60$: $\theta = 30^\circ$. Trap: $45^\circ$ (tan $=$ cot only at 45 when the angles are EQUAL, not complementary).

practice.solution:
Pair $1^\circ$ with $89^\circ$, $2^\circ$ with $88^\circ$, ..., $44^\circ$ with $46^\circ$: 44 pairs each multiplying to 1.

$\tan 45^\circ = 1$ remains in the middle. Product $= 1$.
practice.shortcut: 44 cancelling pairs + $\tan 45^\circ$: product $1$. Trap: $0$ — no factor is zero (tan 0 is absent).

practice.solution:
Complementary cots are reciprocals: $\cot 15^\circ \cot 75^\circ = 1$ (since $15 + 75 = 90$) and $\cot 35^\circ \cot 55^\circ = 1$.

Product $= 1$.
practice.shortcut: Pairs $(15, 75)$ and $(35, 55)$: $1 \times 1 = 1$. Trap: assuming cot-cot pairs don't cancel — complementary cots are still reciprocals.

practice.solution:
$27 + 63 = 90$ and $35 + 55 = 90$: both pairs multiply to 1; $\tan 45^\circ = 1$.

Product $= 1$.
practice.shortcut: Two complementary pairs + the 45° anchor: $1$. Trap: $0$ — no factor vanishes.

practice.solution:
$\sin 76^\circ = \cos 14^\circ$ and $\sin 59^\circ = \cos 31^\circ$ (each pair sums to $90^\circ$).

So the sum $= (\sin^2 14^\circ + \cos^2 14^\circ) + (\sin^2 31^\circ + \cos^2 31^\circ) = 1 + 1 = 2$.
practice.shortcut: Re-pair into two $\sin^2 + \cos^2 = 1$ groups. Trap: $1$ — there are TWO independent pairs here.
Complementary squares cancel. Trap: $3$ (using $\sin^2 60 = \frac34$ for BOTH terms wrongly) or $\frac32$.
$\frac14 + \frac14 + 1 = \frac32$. Trap: $2$ — counting $\tan^2 45^\circ$ twice.
$\frac{m^2 - 1}{2} = \frac12$. Trap: $1$ (forgetting to divide by 2).
$\sqrt{2 - 2} = 0$: at $45^\circ$ the difference vanishes. Trap: $1$ (using $2 - m$ instead of $2 - m^2$).
$\frac{5t - 3}{5t + 3} = \frac{1}{7}$. Trap: $\frac12$ (substituting $t = \frac54$ upside down).
$\frac{3t+1}{t+3} = \frac75$. Trap: $\frac57$ — inverting the final fraction.

practice.q: If $\cot\theta = \frac{21}{20}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\cos\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{21}{29}$. Trap: $\frac{20}{29}$ — that is $\sin\theta$ (cot's numerator is the ADJACENT side).

practice.q: If $\tan\theta = \frac{4}{3}$ ($\theta$ acute), the value of $\sec\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac53$. Trap: $\frac35$ — sec is hyp/ADJ, not adj/hyp.

practice.q: If $\sin\theta - \cos\theta = 0$ and $\theta$ is acute, the value of $\sin\theta$ is:
practice.shortcut: $45^\circ$: $\sin = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}$. Trap: $1$ (that is $\sin 90^\circ$).
$\frac{2t - 1}{2 + 3t} = \frac{3}{22}$. Trap: $\frac{22}{3}$ — the fraction inverted.

practice.solution:
$(\sin\theta - \cos\theta)^2 = 2 - \left(\frac75\right)^2 = 2 - \frac{49}{25} = \frac{1}{25}$.

So $\sin\theta - \cos\theta = \frac15$ (positive root for the acute $\theta$ in the standard exam setup).
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt{2 - m^2} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{25}} = \frac15$. Trap: $\frac{7}{5}$ — that is the given sum itself.
$\sqrt{25} = 5$. Trap: $7$ (adding the coefficients) or $\sqrt7$ (adding squares without the root).

practice.q: The minimum value of $5\sin\theta + 12\cos\theta$ (for all $\theta$) is:
practice.shortcut: $-\sqrt{169} = -13$. Trap: $13$ (forgetting the minus on the minimum).

practice.q: For $0^\circ \le \theta \le 90^\circ$, the maximum value of $\sin\theta + \cos\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
$(\sin\theta + \cos\theta)^2 = 1 + 2\sin\theta\cos\theta \le 1 + 1 = 2$, so the max is $\sqrt2$ at $45^\circ$.

(Or: amplitude of the combination is $\sqrt{1^2+1^2} = \sqrt2$.)
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt{1+1} = \sqrt2$ at $45^\circ$. Trap: $2$ (adding the individual maxima — they occur at different angles).

practice.q: The maximum value of $\sin\theta\cos\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac12$ at $45^\circ$. Trap: $1$ — that is the max of $2\sin\theta\cos\theta$, not of the product.
$\sin 90^\circ = 1$ via the double angle. Trap: $\frac12$ — halving twice.

practice.q: The minimum value of $\tan^2\theta + \cot^2\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:
practice.shortcut: $2$ at $45^\circ$. Trap: $0$ — a positive term and its reciprocal cannot both vanish.

practice.q: The minimum value of $\sec^2\theta + \cosec^2\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac{1}{(\sin\cos)^2} \ge 4$. Trap: $2$ — the bound for $\tan^2 + \cot^2$, not this pair.

practice.q: Which of the following is the largest?
practice.shortcut: $\sin 60^\circ$. Trap: $\cos 60^\circ = \sin 30^\circ$ — they tie at $0.5$, well below $\sin 45^\circ$.

practice.solution: $\sin$ rises and $\cos$ falls; they cross at $45^\circ$. Beyond it, $\sin$ is on top.
practice.shortcut: $\theta > 45^\circ$. Trap: $<$ — the directions of the two functions are easy to swap.

practice.q: The minimum value of $\frac{1}{1 + \sin^2\theta}$ ($\theta$ real) is:
practice.solution:
The fraction is smallest when the denominator is largest: $\sin^2\theta = 1$ gives $1 + 1 = 2$.

Minimum $= \frac12$.
practice.shortcut: $\frac12$ at $\theta = 90^\circ$. Trap: $0$ — the fraction never reaches zero since $1 + \sin^2 \ge 1 > 0$.

practice.q: The minimum value of $8\sin\theta - 15\cos\theta$ over all real $\theta$ is:
practice.solution:
Amplitude $= \sqrt{8^2 + 15^2} = \sqrt{289} = 17$; the expression ranges over $[-17, 17]$.

Minimum $= -17$.
practice.shortcut: $-\sqrt{64 + 225} = -17$. Trap: $17$ (missing the minus) or $-7$ (subtracting the coefficients).

practice.q: The minimum value of $9\tan^2\theta + 4\cot^2\theta$ ($\theta$ acute) is:
practice.shortcut: $2\sqrt{9 \times 4} = 12$. Trap: $13$ ($a + b$) or $6$ ($\sqrt{ab}$, forgot to double).
